hero.name: Gauri
hero.who: a 15-year-old Class 10 student in Nagpur who avoids anything she might fail

story.b: Gauri is in Class 10 at a school in Nagpur, and everyone calls her the smart one in the family. She gets good marks in English and history without much effort. Maths is different. When the teacher announces an optional maths olympiad, Gauri does not even pick up the form. Her friend Tanvi signs up, though her marks are lower. That evening Gauri sits with her algebra homework and skips the hard sums at the bottom of the page. If she gets them wrong, she thinks, everyone will know she was never that smart. She tells her mother she is just not a maths person. Her mother says nothing, but she notices the skipped sums.

ask.q: Gauri skipped the olympiad and the hard sums because failing would feel like proof she is not smart. What belief is holding her back?
o: That she is genuinely bad at maths and should accept it
That ability is fixed, so every test becomes a judgment of who she is
That olympiads are a waste of time for Class 10 students
ask.why: Gauri is not avoiding maths because she cannot learn it. She avoids it because she treats every result as a verdict on her worth. Accepting she is bad at maths, or dismissing the olympiad, keeps that fixed belief safe and stops her from ever growing.

chapters.take: If failing feels like a verdict, you will avoid the very things that help you grow.

story.b: The maths unit test comes back with thirty-one out of fifty circled in red. Gauri's first thought arrives instantly: I am just bad at this. She stuffs the paper into her bag before anyone can see. In the auto home, she remembers something her cousin said about rewriting thoughts. She tries it quietly. Not I am bad at maths, but I have not found the right way to practise yet. It feels a little silly, but it opens a door. At home she spreads out the paper and sorts her mistakes. Most are in quadratic equations, the chapter she rushed through. The problem suddenly looks smaller, almost like a puzzle she can work on.

ask.q: Gauri got thirty-one out of fifty. Which thought will help her improve the most?
o: I need a different way to practise quadratics, so let me find one
I am just not a maths person, and that is fine
The paper was unfair, so the marks do not really count
ask.why: Seeing ability as something she can build turns the mark into a starting point. It points straight to action, like a new way to practise one chapter. Accepting she is not a maths person closes the door, and blaming the paper protects her pride but teaches her nothing.

chapters.take: Ability is something you build, so a low mark is only a starting point.

story.b: Gauri's little brother Ved, who is eight, has been stuck on a hundred-piece jigsaw of a tiger for two days. On Sunday he finally finishes it and runs to show her. The words you are so clever are almost out of her mouth. Then she stops. She remembers how being called the clever one made her scared to try anything hard. Instead she asks him how he did it. Ved explains proudly that he sorted all the edge pieces first, then the orange ones. Gauri tells him she loved how he kept trying new ways when he got stuck. The next week, Ved picks a harder puzzle on his own, a five-hundred-piece map of India.

ask.q: Ved finishes a hard jigsaw. What should Gauri say to help him keep taking on challenges?
o: You are so smart, the cleverest boy in your whole class
Good, but next time try to finish it faster
I loved how you sorted the edges first and kept trying new ways
ask.why: Praising his strategy and effort points to things Ved controls, so he wants to try harder puzzles. Calling him the cleverest gives him a label to protect, which can make him avoid risks. Pushing for speed turns his win into one more test.

chapters.take: Praise what someone did, not what they are, and they will keep trying.

story.h: The filter that did not go
story.b: Gauri and two classmates build a water filter model for the school science exhibition, using sand, charcoal and a cut plastic bottle. The best three projects will go to the district round. Theirs is not picked. Gauri's face burns as the names are read out. Her old instinct is to pretend she never cared. This time she goes to the teacher afterwards and asks what was missing. The teacher explains that the model looked neat, but none of them could explain why the charcoal helps. Gauri writes that down in her rough notebook, along with two more points. The rejection still stings on the cycle ride home, but now she knows exactly what to fix next time.

ask.q: Their model was not selected for the district round. What should Gauri do next?
o: Pretend she never cared about the exhibition anyway
Ask what was missing and note what to change next time
Decide she is not a science person and stick to English
ask.why: A rejection hurts, but it also shows which parts were weak. Asking for feedback turns it into a clear plan for next time. Pretending not to care hides the lesson, and deciding she is not a science person turns one result into a permanent label.

chapters.take: A failure is feedback about what to work on next, not a verdict on you.

story.b: Gauri and Tanvi have been best friends since Class 4. Lately they keep clashing. Tanvi is busy with olympiad coaching and forgets their Saturday plans twice. Gauri feels hurt and stops replying to her messages. Lying awake, she thinks that real best friends should not have to work this hard. Maybe the friendship is just over. Then she notices it is the same old thinking, only now about people. If ability can grow, maybe friendships can too. On Monday, during lunch break, she sits beside Tanvi on the steps near the library and tells her she misses their Saturdays. Tanvi looks relieved. They agree on a new plan: Sunday mornings at the park, after coaching ends.

ask.q: Tanvi keeps forgetting their plans and Gauri feels hurt. What is the healthiest way for Gauri to handle it?
o: Stop talking to her, since a real friend would never need effort
Act like nothing is wrong and quietly find new friends
Talk to her and treat it as a problem they can solve together
ask.why: Believing a good friendship should need no effort turns every clash into proof it is doomed. Talking openly treats the problem as something two people can work through. Silence or quietly drifting away avoids the hurt for now but loses a friend she still cares about.

chapters.take: Good relationships are built through effort, not found ready-made.

story.b: Gauri notices something strange about herself. On the kabaddi team, she loves hard drills. When she gets caught on a raid, she studies how it happened and practises again the next evening. But when her class teacher asks for volunteers to read the news in morning assembly, her stomach drops and her hand stays down. Same girl, two completely different mindsets. She works out what sets off the fixed one: being watched, and the fear of sounding silly. So she takes one small step. She volunteers for a single morning, reads three short headlines and stumbles on one word. Nobody laughs. Her kabaddi coach even gives her a thumbs up from the back row.

ask.q: Gauri trains hard in kabaddi but freezes at the idea of speaking in assembly. What should she do?
o: Notice what triggers her fear and take one small speaking challenge
Accept that she is simply not a public speaker
Wait until she feels fully confident before volunteering
ask.why: Most people have a growth mindset in some areas and a fixed one in others. Spotting her trigger and taking one small step lets her bring her kabaddi attitude to the stage. Accepting a label locks the fear in place, and confidence usually comes after trying, not before.

chapters.take: You can be growth-minded in one place and fixed in another. Notice which is which.

story.h: The form on the notice board
story.b: Three months later, the prelim results come out. Gauri's maths mark has climbed from thirty-one to forty out of fifty. It is not perfect, and that no longer frightens her. She now attempts the hard sums at the bottom of every page first, while her mind is fresh, and circles the ones she gets wrong to discuss with her teacher. When the form for next year's maths olympiad goes up on the notice board, she writes her name right below Tanvi's. Ved has finished his map puzzle and started an even bigger one. On Sunday mornings the two friends still meet at the park, swapping notes and arguing happily about which chapter is the worst.

chapters.take: Growth starts the day you stop protecting a label and start learning.
